analysis.one_liner: Creates a government health plan covering every U.S. resident, financed by premiums and required employer contributions.
analysis.headline: The universal health care bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in three committees until the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created 'AmeriCare,' a public health plan covering every U.S. resident starting in 2010. Benefits would match Medicare, with prescription drug coverage, no deductibles or copays for children, pregnant women, and low-income people, and a cap on out-of-pocket costs for everyone else. It would be financed by premiums from individuals (subsidized for lower incomes), a requirement that employers pay at least 80% of their workers' coverage cost, and federal money for the poorest households. The bill was referred to three House committees in July 2006 and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident would gain guaranteed coverage with Medicare-level benefits, including prescription drugs [S2][S3]. Children under 24, pregnant women, and people under 200% of the poverty line would pay no deductibles or coinsurance, and would get extras like eyeglasses, hearing aids, and dental care [S3]. Families between 200% and 500% of poverty would have their total premiums and out-of-pocket costs capped at 5-7.5% of income [S3]. Everyone would get an annual out-of-pocket cap of $2,500 ($4,000 per family), and providers could not bill patients beyond the plan's payment [S3]. Low-income households below 300% of poverty would receive premium subsidies, with free coverage for those below 200% [S3]. Medicare itself would be upgraded to match AmeriCare's benefits [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Every U.S. resident, especially low-income families

how_it_helps.text: Makes every U.S. resident eligible for health benefits equivalent to Medicare hospital and medical coverage, including prescription drugs, effective January 1, 2010.

Eliminates deductibles and coinsurance for children under 24, pregnant women, and people below 200% of the poverty line, and adds eyeglasses, hearing aids, well-child care, and preventive dental care for children and the poor.
Caps out-of-pocket costs at $2,500 per person ($4,000 per family) per year, and caps combined premiums plus cost-sharing at 5-7.5% of income for families earning between 200% and 500% of poverty.
Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prescription drug prices with manufacturers, instead of the current law prohibiting negotiation under Medicare's drug benefit.

Requires employers to contribute at least 80% of the cost of coverage for each employee, exempting employers with fewer than 100 employees until 2012, and exempts employers already paying 80% of a private group plan.
Bans providers from balance billing patients, so enrollees could not be charged more than the program's payment rate.
Expands Medicare benefits to match AmeriCare, including a single deductible, uniform coinsurance, and an out-of-pocket limit.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would bear a new obligation to pay at least 80% of each employee's premium unless they already cover 80% of a private group plan. Individuals would owe income-based premiums, collected through wage withholding like a tax, though fully subsidized below 300% of poverty. Federal taxpayers would fund the low-income premium subsidies from general revenues. States would have to keep paying their 2006-level Medicaid and SCHIP contributions. Private insurers would lose the market for coverage the public plan replaces, and drug manufacturers would face negotiated prices.

drawbacks.text: Employers with 100 or more employees would owe at least 80% of each worker's premium cost, a significant new payroll obligation unless they already provide equivalent coverage, which could reduce hiring or wages.

People who keep private group plans rather than enrolling would forgo AmeriCare, and employers keeping private plans could face a surcharge if the Secretary finds it necessary to prevent healthier people from leaving the public plan.
The bill leaves Medicare Advantage-style private health plans in place as an enrollment option rather than creating a purely single-payer system, preserving a private-plan role in the public program.
The cost of low-income premium subsidies depends on annual appropriations from general revenues, which Congress could decline to provide.
States would be required to keep paying into the program at their 2006 Medicaid and SCHIP levels as a condition of their residents receiving coverage, limiting states' fiscal flexibility.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are very large: universal coverage, no cost-sharing for children and the poor, and a hard cap on out-of-pocket spending, funded by employer contributions and income-based premiums rather than new broad taxes. The costs are real but conventional for this approach: a mandate on large employers, premiums for higher-income enrollees, continued state Medicaid spending, and federal subsidies for the poorest households. The design keeps private employer plans and supplemental insurance alongside the public program rather than replacing them, which softens disruption but also preserves administrative duplication.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and then to a subcommittee, and none of them ever took it up; it died when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the AmeriCare Health Care Act of 2006 in the House on July 25, 2006, near the end of the two-year session, joined by 36 cosponsors, all Democrats.

The bill was referred to three committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce — a multi-committee referral that requires any of them to act before the bill can move.
On September 28, 2006, part of the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, where it stayed.

No committee held a markup, no vote ever occurred in the House, and the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, killing the bill under the rule that legislation does not carry over between Congresses.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The people and groups better off because the bill died are employers who would have owed the 80% contribution, private health insurers who would have lost the market the public plan replaced, and drug manufacturers who would have faced government price negotiation. The roughly 47 million Americans without coverage in 2006, for whom the bill was written, gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All 36 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican supported the bill, and the Republican-controlled committees of the 109th Congress never acted on it.

industries.note: AmeriCare would replace private coverage for everyone not in an employer group plan, shrinking the individual insurance market, but the bill lets employer group plans continue as the opt-out route and creates a new certified market for AmeriCare supplemental policies with guaranteed renewability and minimum payout rules. Insurers keep the employer-based system but lose the standalone market a public plan can cover more cheaply.

The bill requires the Secretary to negotiate drug purchase prices with manufacturers and to pay for outpatient drugs on a fee schedule instead of the prices set under the 2003 Medicare drug law. Negotiated federal purchasing would lower drug costs for patients and taxpayers at the expense of manufacturer revenues.

Employers with 100 or more employees would owe at least 80% of each worker's coverage cost, with small employers exempt until 2012. Employers already paying 80% of a private group plan would be exempt, so the mandate falls hardest on businesses that currently provide nothing.

Universal enrollment would bring millions of previously uninsured patients into a program paying Medicare rates, sharply reducing uncompensated care. Providers would give up balance billing — charging patients above the program's payment — but gain a guaranteed payer for nearly everyone.
